title: Machine-learning mapping finds broader preservation of pre-glacial landscapes across Arctic Canada and Greenland
summary: A random-forest model using six terrain morphometrics from ArcticDEM classified glacial erosional styles across Arctic Canada and Greenland. The map indicates that regions with little or no glacial erosion, and thus potentially preserved pre-glacial landscape fragments, occur more widely than previous mapping recognized; it also finds distinct morphologies between Greenland and Canada. The authors infer that inherited topography, ice dynamics, latitude and geology help shape these patterns.

evidence.tested: A random-forest model using six terrain morphometrics from ArcticDEM classified glacial erosional styles across Arctic Canada and Greenland.
evidence.unknown: The paper reports validation accuracy of about 79.5% (±4.6%) and notes low classification probabilities in some areas, where training coverage or coarse classes may limit confidence. “Little or no glacial erosion” is a model classification interpreted as possible preservation of pre-glacial terrain, not direct dating or field confirmation of every mapped tile. Proposed controls such as ice dynamics and basal hydrology are interpretations, not demonstrated causal mechanisms.
evidence.ai_role: The random forest classified ArcticDEM tiles using six elevation-derived morphometric variables, assigning class probabilities at continental scale and producing model-derived feature-importance estimates. This enabled a quantitative revision of prior qualitative landscape maps and the reported finding that minimally glacially modified terrain is more widespread than previously mapped.
